\begin{definition}[Two-quantifier efficient verification]
\lean{Randomized.InSigma2}
\statementsource{Vad12}{
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p059-b006,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p059-b007,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p060-b001,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p060-b002,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p061-b001,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p061-b002
}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p013-b002}
\label{Randomized.InSigma2}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.polyLen}
A language $L$ belongs to the class defined by an efficient two-witness verifier if
there are a verifier $N$ and natural numbers $a_1,k_1,a_2,k_2$ such that $N$ is
efficient according to $E$. For every input $x$, membership in $L$ is equivalent to the
existence of a string $u$ of length $a_1+k_1|x|$ such that, for every string $v$ of
length $a_2+k_2|x|$, the verifier outputs true on $(x,u,v)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Complement of the two-quantifier class]
\lean{Randomized.InPi2}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p061-b002}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p013-b002}
\label{Randomized.InPi2}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.InSigma2}
A language $L$ belongs to the class defined by the complement condition if its
complement belongs to the class defined by an efficient two-witness verifier.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Shifted OR verifier]
\lean{Randomized.shiftOrVerifier}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p060-b001}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{
  pdf-26d95080dbde-p013-b003,
  pdf-26d95080dbde-p014-b001
}
\label{Randomized.shiftOrVerifier}
\leanok
Given a Boolean verifier $M$ and functions $p,k:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$, define a
verifier on strings $(x,u,v)$ as follows: it outputs true if and only if, for some
integer $i$ with $0\le i<k(|x|)$, $M$ outputs true on $x$ and the string obtained by
taking the length-$p(|x|)$ segment of $u$ beginning at position $i p(|x|)$ and XORing it
bit by bit with $v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Closure under shifted OR verification]
\lean{Randomized.ClosedUnderShiftOr}
\statementsource{Vad12}{
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p060-b001,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p060-b002,
  pdf-bf2ce5422088-p061-b001
}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p014-b001}
\label{Randomized.ClosedUnderShiftOr}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.boolVerifier, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.shiftOrVerifier}
The verifier model $E$ is closed under shifted OR verification if, for every Boolean
verifier $M$ and all natural numbers $a,k,a',k'$, whenever $M$ is efficient according to
$E$, the shifted OR verifier built from $M$ using the polynomial length functions
determined by $(a,k)$ and $(a',k')$ is an efficient two-witness verifier according to
$E$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Zip of indexed sequences]
\lean{Randomized.zipWith_ofFn}
\label{Randomized.zipWith_ofFn}
\leanok
\difficulty{3}
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be types, let $m$ be a natural number, let
$f:\alpha\to\beta\to\gamma$, and let $a$ and $b$ be sequences indexed by
$\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ with values in $\alpha$ and $\beta$, respectively. Zipping their
lists of values with $f$ gives the list whose $i$th entry is $f(a(i),b(i))$ for $0\le
i<m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance under a fixed bitwise mask]
\lean{Randomized.randProb_xor_right}
\label{Randomized.randProb_xor_right}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.randProb, Randomized.zipWith_ofFn}
\difficulty{5}
For a natural number $m$, a bit string $c$ of length $m$, and a decidable property $P$
of finite bit strings, choose a uniformly random bit string $r$ of length $m$. The
probability that $P$ holds of the bitwise XOR of $c$ and $r$ is equal to the probability
that $P$ holds of $r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance Under a Fixed XOR Mask]
\lean{Randomized.randProb_xor_left}
\label{Randomized.randProb_xor_left}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.randProb, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_xor_right, Randomized.zipWith_ofFn}
\difficulty{4}
Let $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $c$ be a Boolean vector of length $m$, and let $P$ be any
property of finite Boolean lists. If a uniformly random Boolean list of length $m$ is
combined entrywise by exclusive-or with $c$, the probability that the resulting list
satisfies $P$ equals the probability that the original random list satisfies $P$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exponential bound for natural numbers]
\lean{Randomized.shift_count_lt_two_pow}
\label{Randomized.shift_count_lt_two_pow}
\leanok
\difficulty{5}
For natural numbers $A$ and $X$ with $1\le X$, one has $(19A+20)X<2^{(A+7)X}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exponential tail bound]
\lean{Randomized.const_tail_bound}
\label{Randomized.const_tail_bound}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.one_sub_pow_le_half_pow, Randomized.polyLen}
\difficulty{4}
For all natural numbers $b,e,n$, let $P(a,k,n)=a(n+1)^k$. Then
$2\bigl(1-4(1/6)^2\bigr)^{\lfloor P(18b+18,e,n)/2\rfloor}\le (1/2)^{P(b,e,n)}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Concrete error reduction by majority]
\lean{Randomized.amplify_concrete}
\label{Randomized.amplify_concrete}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.ClosedUnderMajority, Randomized.blockCount, Randomized.boolVerifier, Randomized.const_tail_bound, Randomized.majorityVerifier, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.randProb, Randomized.randProb_bool_false, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_mono, Randomized.randProb_not, Randomized.randProb_tail_le}
\difficulty{6}
Let $E$ be a verifier model closed under majority, and let $L$ be a language with an
efficient verifier $M_0$ using $a_0(n+1)^{k_0}$ random bits, whose acceptance
probability on members and rejection probability on nonmembers are each at least $2/3$.
For any natural numbers $b,e$, there is an efficient verifier $M$ whose acceptance
probability on members and rejection probability on nonmembers are each at least
$1-(1/2)^{b(n+1)^e}$, using $(18b+18)a_0(n+1)^{e+k_0}$ random bits on inputs of length
$n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[An Element Outside a Proper Subset]
\lean{Randomized.exists_notMem_of_card_lt}
\label{Randomized.exists_notMem_of_card_lt}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and let $S$ be a finite subset of $\alpha$. If
$|S|<|\alpha|$, then there is an element of $\alpha$ that does not belong to $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[BPP Languages in the Second Existential Level]
\lean{Randomized.bpp_subset_sigma2}
\label{Randomized.bpp_subset_sigma2}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.ClosedUnderMajority, Randomized.ClosedUnderShiftOr, Randomized.InBPP, Randomized.InSigma2, Randomized.amplify_concrete, Randomized.blockCount, Randomized.card_univ_bitstrings, Randomized.exists_notMem_of_card_lt, Randomized.exists_ofFn_eq, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.randProb, Randomized.randProb_blockCount, Randomized.randProb_bool_false, Randomized.randProb_le_one, Randomized.randProb_xor_left, Randomized.randProb_xor_right, Randomized.shiftOrVerifier, Randomized.shift_count_lt_two_pow}
\difficulty{7}
Let $E$ be a verifier model closed under polynomial majority amplification and under the
verifier that accepts when at least one of polynomially many runs accepts after its
random bits are combined by bitwise exclusive-or with a second witness. If $L$ has an
efficient randomized verifier accepting members and rejecting nonmembers with
probability at least $2/3$, then there is an efficient two-witness verifier $N$ and
polynomial bounds $p_1(n)=a_1(n+1)^{k_1}$ and $p_2(n)=a_2(n+1)^{k_2}$ such that, for
every Boolean word $x$, membership in $L$ is equivalent to the existence of a Boolean
word $u$ of length $p_1(|x|)$ for which every Boolean word $v$ of length $p_2(|x|)$
satisfies $N(x,u,v)=\mathrm{true}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[BPP lies in the second-level classes]
\lean{Randomized.sipser_gacs}
\label{Randomized.sipser_gacs}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.ClosedUnderMajority, Randomized.ClosedUnderNot, Randomized.ClosedUnderShiftOr, Randomized.InBPP, Randomized.InBPP.compl, Randomized.InPi2, Randomized.InSigma2, Randomized.bpp_subset_sigma2}
\difficulty{1}
Let $E$ be a verifier model closed under polynomially many repetitions followed by
majority vote, under negating a verifier's answer, and under the shift-or construction.
If a language $L$ has a polynomial-time randomized verifier that uses polynomially many
random bits and answers correctly with probability at least $2/3$ on every input, then
$L$ belongs to both the second-level existential and universal polynomial-hierarchy
classes defined using polynomial-length witnesses and polynomial-time predicates.
\end{theorem}
